title: Why Principals Don't Praise
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explores why so many principals fail to praise or acknowledge their teachers despite expecting teachers to praise students constantly. He offers three explanations: some are simply poor leaders who mistake distance and unavailability for authority; some let ego or insecurity about their position get in the way of genuine appreciation; and many simply don't understand what effective classroom management actually looks like, so they avoid direct, substantive feedback in favor of vague talk about policies and rewards systems. He contrasts these principals with two he personally worked under who praised generously and specifically, were visible and accessible, and treated staff as people first. His closing message reassures teachers that an unresponsive principal reflects the principal's own shortcomings, not the teacher's worth.
points: Identifies three reasons principals often fail to praise teachers: poor leadership, ego or insecurity, and lack of classroom management expertise.
Cites research linking employee recognition to job satisfaction and cascading effects on school culture.
Notes many principals were never especially skilled classroom managers themselves and avoid substantive feedback as a result.
Contrasts weak principals with two personally experienced examples who praised generously, specifically, and visibly.
Reassures teachers that an unresponsive principal reflects the principal's own shortcomings, not the teacher's worth.
quotes: That doesn’t mean that it doesn’t hurt when you’re ignored or your good work goes unnoticed.
According to research, recognition is one of the biggest keys to job satisfaction. When an employee feels valued and appreciated, they’re more motivated and confident in their abilities.
Few principals are experts in classroom management. Fewer still were experts when they were in the classroom.

As a new teacher, low in confidence, one former boss used to leave cards and notes in my mailbox assuring me I was doing well. She would point out specifically what she liked, guiding me down the right and effective path.
They were people, first and foremost, and knew that they were the chief engine that drove positive school culture, morale, and pride in being a Ram or Eagle or Viking.
It isn’t about you and your shortcomings. It’s about them and theirs.
